parole.testo: A conflation of two senses: one meaning "look", from Danish skue (“to look”), another meaning "truly", from Danish sgu (“intensifier word”).

parole.significato: to have a speech disorder in which one pronounces the Icelandic "R" sound as a uvular guttural R
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish skråle.
Borrowed from Danish skidt, from Low German schiet, schitt.

parole.significato: a hit song, a popular pop song
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish slager, from German Schlager (“hit song”), derived from schlagen (“to hit”). Attested since 1929. Cognate with slá.
Borrowed from Danish slap, from Middle Low German slap.
From sleikja (“to lick”) + pinni (“pin, stick”); calque of Danish slikkepind, slikpind.

parole.significato: under the weather, poorly, feeling somewhat weak
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish sløj.

Borrowed from Danish slem, which borrowed it from Middle Low German slim (“bent, crooked”), from Old Saxon *slimb, from Proto-West Germanic *slimb, from Proto-Germanic *slimbaz (“slanted, crooked”). Possibly related to Lithuatian slim̃pti (“to sneak, stroll”).

parole.significato: to stop, bring to an end
parole.testo: 17th century, from Danish slutte.

parole.significato: bib (item of clothing for babies tied around their neck to protect their clothes from getting dirty when eating)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish smække, first attested in c. 1900.
Borrowed from Danish sminke. Compare German schminken.
Borrowed from Danish snaps, from Low German snapps. Cf. German Schnaps.
Borrowed from Danish snedig using spelling pronunciation. Compare sniðugur, which was phonetically borrowed from the same Danish word.

parole.significato: pacifier, dummy (device for babies to suck on)
parole.testo: From snuða (“to trick”), from Danish snyde (“to trick”).
Borrowed from Danish sådan (“such”).
Borrowed from Danish spøg.
Borrowed from Danish splejse, from English splice and Dutch splitten. The meaning of paying for someone else comes from taking the other person's receipt and "splicing" it to yours.

parole.significato: a tram, a streetcar; (a passenger vehicle for public use that runs on tracks in the road)
parole.testo: Addapted from Danish sporvogn. Compound of spor (“rail”) + vagn (“cart”).

parole.significato: a clear, strong solution of alcohol
parole.testo: Attested since the 19th century. Borrowed from Danish sprit, from German Sprit, from French esprit, from Latin spīritus.
From Danish sprog, from Middle Low German sprâke, from Old Saxon sprāka. Cognate with Swedish språk.

parole.significato: an earflap on a hat that may be tied under the jaw
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish spjæld, from Old Norse spjald, speld, from Proto-Germanic *speldą.
Borrowed from Danish spinat.

Borrowed from Danish stakit, borrowed from Middle Low German staket or stakit, borrowed from Middle French estachette, derived from Old French estache (“pole, stake”), a Germanic borrowing cognate with Icelandic staki, English stake from Proto-Germanic *stakô (“pole, stick, stake”) from Proto-Indo-E
Adapted from Danish standart, from Old French estandart.
Borrowed from Danish statist, from German Statist.
Borrowed from Danish statistik.

parole.significato: service (set of matching dishes or untensils)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish stel.

parole.significato: to fit, to agree with, to correspond to, to coincide with
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish stemme, from Middle Low German stemmen. Related to stemma (“melody [for a ballad]”) (4).
Borrowed from Danish stemme (“voice; musical part; vote”).
Borrowed from Danish stikkelsbær. By surface analysis, stikill + ber.
Borrowed from Danish stempel.

parole.significato: to stop, to come to a stop
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish stoppe.

parole.significato: to iron, to press; to pass an iron over clothing to remove creases.
parole.testo: From Danish stryge (past strøg).

parole.significato: knitting which alternates between flat and raised; for example, the cuff of a sock, or the wrist section of a glove or…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish strop.
Borrowed from Danish stylte.
Borrowed from Danish styrte, from Middle Low German storten, from Old Saxon *sturtian, from Proto-West Germanic *sturtijan.
Borrowed from Danish støtte (“pillar, statue, aid”), from Middle Low German stutte (“support; staff, stick”).
Borrowed from Danish stads.
Borrowed from Danish stole.

parole.significato: a person who has graduated from a gymnasium (menntaskóli, a secondary school level for 16–19 year olds)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish student or Middle Low German student, from Latin.

Literally, “black death”, compounding svartur (“black”) + dauði (“death”); calque of Danish den sorte død, sortedød and Swedish svarta döden, svartedöden since the 18th century, from Old Danish and Old Swedish, first attested in Swedish swarta dödhen (1540), svarthe döden (1555), then as a historica
Borrowed from Danish svær (16th century), itself from Norwegian svár with influence from German schwer; ultimately from Proto-Germanic *swēraz.
Borrowed from Danish svindel, from German Schwindel.
Borrowed from Danish svindle, from German schwindeln.

parole.significato: to work like a charm, to work very well (for solving an issue)
parole.testo: Composed of svín- + virka. Although the literal meaning is “works like a pig”, “svín-” is here a prefix that is used for emphasis, a practice borrowed from Danish svine- (e.g. svineheld). Compare also German Schweine- (e.g. schweinekalt (“very cold”)) and other prefixes such as Icelandic hundleiðinl
Borrowed from Danish suite (and English suite in the sense “hotel apartment”, etc.), from French suite, from Latin sequita, secuta, from sequor (“follow”).

Borrowed from Danish sukker, from Middle High German zucker, from Old High German zucker, from Old Italian zucchero, from Arabic سُكَّر (sukkar), from Early Modern Persian شکر (šakar), from Middle Persian 𐭱𐭪𐭥 (šakar), from Sanskrit शर्करा (śárkarā).

Borrowed from Danish chokolade, from German Schokolade, from Dutch chocolade, from Spanish chocolate, from Classical Nahuatl chocolātl.
Borrowed from Danish syren, from Latin syrinx.

Borrowed from Danish tak, from Old Norse þǫkk (whence inherited Icelandic þökk), from Proto-Germanic *þankō, *þankaz. Cognates include Faroese and Norwegian takk, Danish tak, Swedish tack, English thank, West Frisian tank, Dutch dank and German Dank.
Borrowed from Danish tante, from French tante, from Latin amita.
Borrowed from Danish tøj.
Constructed on the basis of Danish integrere, ultimately from Latin integrō.
Borrowed from Danish temmelig. Cognate with German ziemlich.

From timbur (“timber”) + maður (“man”). The sense ‘hangover’ is a Semantic loan from Danish tømmermænd (“a hangover”). The oldest attestation of timburmenn in the sense "hangover" in the Orðabók Háskólans is from an issue of Fjallkonan from 1891 which goes as follows: : Margar tegundir kaffibrauðs .
Probably taken from Danish tja.
Borrowed from Danish tomme.

parole.significato: a threeway, a threesome (a sexual act involving three people)

Borrowed from Danish trække, from Proto-Germanic *trakjaną.
From Danish tragt, from Middle Low German trechtäre, trechter, from Old Saxon trahtari, from Proto-West Germanic *trahtārī, from Late Latin tractārius, from Latin trāiectōrium.
From Danish tromme.

parole.significato: chewing gum (a sweetened flavoured preparation of chicle, made for chewing)
parole.testo: A calque of Danish tyggegummi, equivalent to tyggja (“chew”) + gúmmí (“gum, rubber”).
A neologism derived from tæki (“a tool”) + -ni (nominal suffix). Phono-semantic matching of Danish teknik. Coined by Dr. Björn Bjarnason from Viðfjörður in 1912.
Borrowed from Danish tundra, from Russian ту́ндра (túndra).

parole.significato: discussing in private; for two people to discuss without others present
parole.testo: Literally, “under four eyes”. Cognate or calque of Danish under fire øjne, a cognate of German unter vier Augen. Also compare Dutch onder vier ogen, Indonesian empat mata, Yiddish אונטער פֿיר אויגן (unter fir oygn), Hebrew בארבע עיניים, Italian a quattr'occhi and French entre quatre yeux.
Calque of Danish opleve; equivalent to upp (“up”) + lifa (“to live”).

Borrowed from Danish vampyr, via German Vampir from a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian vàmpīr.
Borrowed from Danish vase c, which is borrowed from French vase m, ultimately from Latin vās n (“vessel, vase”).
Borrowing from Danish vask.

Borrowed from Danish væske, from Middle Low German veske.

Borrowed from Danish vinkel (“angle”).
Borrowed from Danish virke from Old Norse virkja, from Proto-Germanic *wirkijaną.
Borrowed from Danish viskestykke.

Borrowed from Danish være i sit es, from German. "Ess" is from Latin esse (“state, condition”). Ásgeir Blöndal suggests the phrase may be influenced by French être à son aise, cognate with English at ease.

Borrowed from Danish ohm, from the surname of German physicist Georg Ohm.

Via another European language, perhaps Danish, from Latin uncia.

Adapted from Danish drue, from Middle Low German drūve (“bunch”), from Proto-West Germanic *þrūbō.
Borrowed from Danish banan, from English banana, from a Romance language (either Portuguese banana or Spanish banana), from Wolof banaana.
